projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The entire interview with Emily Hays was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div2.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of an audiotaped interview with Emily Hays, conducted by Wellon Lee on March 22, 2002, on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The interview was transcribed and processed by Leslie A. Kesterson.

The reader should bear in mind that she or he is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of places, names, foreign words and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: This is Wellon Lee. I'm going to interview Emily Hays. It is March 22, 2002.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What was your spouse's name in wartime occupation?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: James V. Caw (ph). His occupation was a student.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What did he do during the war? What war -- what was his wartime service?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, he was a marine pilot, and he served in the South Pacific.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Okay. Where and when were you married?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: We were married in Selma, Alabama, on March 20, 1944.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How long was -- was Pop absent from home?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Almost a year.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And did you see him during the time?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. He was sent overseas. I saw him, and we went -- I went to two different places where he served during -- before he was sent there. His squadron was sent overseas.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: We went to Morehead City, North Carolina and Greenville, North Carolina. He served his time at Cherry Point.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you have any children while he was gone to war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No children.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Where did you live at the time of the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: When we -- I followed him after we were married. I followed him to Greenville and then to Morehead City because he was -- Cherry Point didn't have facilities -- living facilities except at the two different cities that were close by. So I was with him at that time until the squadron was sent overseas. And then I went back to Selma.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And lived --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: And lived there while he was gone a year.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did you work while he was gone?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Yes, I did. I worked at the bank, Selma National Bank. And I had applied for the runner job, but it was taken by another wife whose husband was gone.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Were most of the people that you worked with wives of soldiers?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. There were none. They were all older people.
And the older ones that -- were lawyers at the bank. But I ended up being a secretary to the president. They put up with me.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What about unions? Was the bank unionized? I don't know much about unions.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Yeah, I don't think at that time -- I don't know. I didn't -- I was not aware of a union at that time --

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: -- to the bank. I'm not sure.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did you have friends that participated in the war contribution, wartime work-wise?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: I was friends mostly with the wives of those -- whose husbands were in the service and overseas at the time. We didn't do any -- actually, we didn't do the -- we didn't have any organizations there in Selma, other than just to get together to console one another because they were all gone.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How long were some of your friends' husbands gone for?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, gosh. Several years.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: And we ended up losing a couple of them, husbands at the time. It was quite an experience, really.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What were your general feelings about the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, it was devastating. It really was. You're young and you -- I mean, we were young at the time, and we were daredevils, more or less. And I remember when the boys would go on the flights from Cherry Point, they'd come over the house and buzz the house, things like that that they did that they shouldn't have done. It thrilled us. It gave us a lift of the day and we knew they were all right.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: And that was the main thing.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What about -- were there many people that were adamantly against the war, or were you-all just supportive?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: We were supportive. We grieved and we worried and we complained, but we were supportive.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: In what ways did the war change your daily activities?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, completely. I mean, you worried constantly. You grieved constantly. You -- because you couldn't be with them.

You'd hear -- all you were concerned about were your friends and those that were in the middle of things. You couldn't hear from them at the time when they were overseas. And when my husband was first sent, he had fallen off of the wing of a plane that was on the ground. And he had -- was bleeding from his kidneys. But he wanted to go with his squadron. So he said, "No, I'm not staying." He would not go back to the hospital. He went -- so when he got to Okinawa, the first thing that happened was there was a -- not a tornado. What do they call it? A typhoon hit, and it blew away the medical supplies. So there was no way to take tests or do anything.
So he had a rougher time, and I worried more about him.
Letters we got, you -- they couldn't say anything. They couldn't tell you where they were or what they were doing.
And if they tried to, it was blacked out. So you just had to pray a lot, and we did.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How often would you get letters from Pop?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Not too often.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Not often enough.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Not often enough. Not half often enough.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What social activities were you involved in? Were there organized social activities?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Well, not really, no. We didn't -- not as a couple when he was there in the service because we had fun getting together with other groups. But we had no activities that were organized.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Were there activities for the wives aboard?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Not at the time. There was not much that was going on as far as entertaining. We -- when the boys were available -- and they didn't fly nights. They didn't have much night flight when they were in the states. So we got together with couples. And they did have the officers quarters that they had a place you could go at the -- on the base that you could meet your friends.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What were weddings like during the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It was kind of rough because there was so many friends that were gone that -- it wasn't like the present day where you can get your friends together at the drop of a hat. Wives would be there or maybe a few couples. But the big weddings were very far -- few and far between. And presents -- gifts were hard to come by because of the war efforts. They -- I know the brides picking out their silver and their china and those things were extremely limited. And it took years to -- to acquire enough. You had to settle for _________.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How much did you hear about from the media about the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, constantly. We had wonderful reporters that -- marvelous through the radio and television. It was marvelous, it really was. At least we felt that we had some contact. We knew what was going on. Sometimes that was good, and sometimes it was bad. But at least we were well informed.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did you ever worry about which side was winning?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. You just have to put your faith in the Lord and know that you are going to win, and we did.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Was there an overwhelming general sense of anxiety, or was, you know, your faith -- we talked a little bit about everyone's feelings.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Feelings of mine -- you had to have faith. You had to trust. And there again I can say that we -- there were so many young people in the service at that time just out of high school and early college. And we -- we didn't -- we didn't -- we didn't have the prayer groups that you have now.

We prayed and we met and we went to church, but there were not groups that supported groups as we have now. There is a lot that they've learned through the years on helping families cope with what was ahead.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And having a community?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did you ever talk to Pop's parents --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, constantly.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: -- during the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: They were there in Selma as I was. So, of course, I was right in contact every -- we talked every -- saw them every day. Selma is a small town. It was -- it was wonderful to have my family and his family.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: So was Pop in Okinawa for that year? He was overseas for a year?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And when he came back, did other husbands come back?
Or was he -- was he one of the first --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. Their -- all their squadron was returned at the time. And when he was out of the service, then that was when we went to the hospital and he had his kidney removed.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Oh, I didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Uh-huh. That was -- it was a necessity. But he didn't want to have it done by -- in the service because you could not choose the doctors. They had -- they didn't have as many specialists then in those -- in those '40s that they have now where they are certainly capable and you'd have confidence in them. We felt it was better for him to be busted out of the service and have it done at home by someone who we knew was capable.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did his injury affect him during the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Apparently not. He flew just like all the rest of them. But he had his buddies, and they had flown together and trained together as a squadron. And that's -- they worked together. And he just -- they did fine.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What were some of the wartime shortages? You mentioned rations.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, my. I know the main thing was the rations, and it affected so many of the people, the working people, the older than our age at that time. Tires and gasoline. Oh, it was just pitiful. I worked at the rationing board, and they rationed -- it was only 320 miles that they gave you gasoline for. And a traveling salesman had no chance. They couldn't do anything. There was so much on the black market then, too, because -- because of the shortage, and people were trying to make a living. And I never will forget when we were going to the first squadron, when we were going to Cherry Point. And my mother-in-law and I were driving a second-hand car that we had to have. Because we had taken the train, open hair, no -- no screens on the windows and the soot coming in. We rode the train to Cherry Point. But when she and I were going to -- for me to stay with -- to live, we had four blowouts on the tires because they were second-hand tires. And -- but we finally got to where we were going.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: You learned quickly how to change a tire?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: We learned -- well, we didn't have that many. We had to ask the rationing boards along the way to help us out. ANd becuase we were service related, it worked out. But it was -- it was really terriffic.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Would they distribute -- how would you find out about the rations, just sort of when you went?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, every -- everybody knew what was rationed.
They -- first they rationed the gasoline and the tires. And then as far as the food went, we had sugar rations, no sugar.

I mean, we were limited. And that affected the cookies and cakes and everything that people would buy. But the one thing that hurt women more than anything else was shoes and stockings. You could not buy stockings. And it was pretty rough. But we made out. You know, you learned to roll with the punches and you complained about it, but that's okay.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Character building.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: It makes you who you are today, I know.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Well, you have to learn, don't you? Sometimes the hard way.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What were some of your most memorable experiences? Do you have memories that just stick in your head?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, how wonderful, wonderful, wonderful the people were that we -- where we lived. They were -- everything was for the service man. Oh, just absolutely wonderful people.
They had you to dinner, they took you in, they helped you find a place to live. And it was just like small town, just wrapping their arms around you, opening and welcome.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Was this in Selma?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. This -- well, I'm sure Selma people did, but my experience was in the two cities -- towns that we lived. It was great.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What about some other memories that you have of it?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Of deaths. And in the squadron, the first squadron was pretty rough to take. One of the boys went in on the flights, and that affected everybody so much. But it also helped us grow. And it really -- we realized what we were facing. It made us mature in a hurry, it really did.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Was Pop able to share his grief with you over letters, or could he not talk --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Well, this was when we were still in the states.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: So it was quite an experience. We lost two from the states. And we had went ahead and shared a house with one couple, and he was lost overseas. So it was -- it is pretty heart wrenching.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What did his wife do?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: She went back to Richmond, Virginia, and we kept in touch for years. And Pop and I went by to see his mother at one time when we were there. But I have lost track now. She remarried, and I don't know what happened. But we lost some good friends, some close associations with people.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: I can't imagine how difficult that is.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It is pretty rough. It really was. But that is what everybody was sharing. And even though we didn't have support groups and -- we shared with one another, and that way you got through.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What about church services?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: They had them on the base. And wherever we went, we found a little church.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Was there sort of a common theme throughout church services because of the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It was, generally.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: On how to cope or --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Well, not that. See -- well, in those days they didn't -- they didn't have these support groups that really mean so much today. You just were with people and shared your griefs and you worked it out yourself more or less. Never have there ever been -- if you want to take advantage of it, if you're not such a private person, if you can't -- share what you are feeling. But it was -- it was a real experience meeting -- I had not lived or been out of Selma, a small town.

And this did -- yes, in all of that and to other cities. I don't mean that I had never been anywhere. But I had never lived anywhere else until the service. And you run into people -- all kinds of people. But you also find and dwell on the people that really lean towards you and you know are good folks.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Where were you when we -- when you heard the news of victory?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, we were in Selma, of course. And it was just -- just wonderful. The girls -- the -- quote, the girls -- and we did, we had -- on the street that I lived, there were six of us. And they lived right across the street from each other. Seven of us. And it was just fabulous to have that much with all of our boys gone.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And what about --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: So we whooped and hollered and cried and screamed and had a real celebration.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How long was that after Pop had been gone?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: That was the year.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And he returned just shortly afterwards?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What was it like when he returned?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, we met him in Pensacola, and I was real selfish.

I wanted to go myself. I didn't want the in-laws to go. But the in-laws did go and, in fact, they took me. And we had two hotel rooms, and it was just -- oh, it was wonderful. We met him, and he was fine when we got there. And I was so -- I felt so guilty because I wanted to share and yet I didn't. I wanted him to myself.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Was he changed when he came back?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: He was not, really. He -- it served him well. I mean, he did good.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: He is tough.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: He is tough.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Emotionally?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: He really did. But it was quite an experience.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How would you say that the war influenced your ways of thinking after it ended?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, it made me a stronger person. I knew I could do some things that I hadn't thought I could. I knew I could take care of myself if I had to. It made me appreciate people more and feelings more. I think it made me a better -- a much better person if I hadn't of experienced it.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Is there anything else that you'd just like to share that you want other people to know that they might not know?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: I can't think of anything that you just have to have.
You have to trust and hang in, appreciate what you've got while you've got it.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: I'm so glad I have gotten to hear this.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What about Pop going back to school after he came back from the war?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: When he first came back, of course, he -- he ended up with surgery, kidney surgery. So after he recouped from that, he went back to the university and he completed his education at the University of Alabama.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: He completed his education there and then entered law school there. So he -- that took a good many years. At the time he finished law school, we had two children. And we moved to Birmingham, Alabama at that point, and he went into accounting. Then he took his accounting exams and bar exams, of course, and all of that. So he had a duel degree.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Was that from the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It paid for some of it, yes.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did he work while he was in law school, or did you work?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. I didn't work. I had two children --

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Oh, that's right.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: -- at that time. So he -- he didn't work, except a little. And I can't remember what organization he worked for at that time. But it was just a short, you know, two or three hours. But it -- it paid off great. So he ended up with a degree in accounting and a law degree, which tax accounting was what he was interested in at that point.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: After the war, did people sit around and talk about it?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Oh, constantly and the experiences that they had.

They always -- when you got the menfolks together, that was the first thing they wanted to brush over, where were you and what did you do. There were always contacts, people that wanted to call one another. They had been together and gone through so much together, they couldn't turn loose immediately. So it was wonderful that they hadn't -- that they had friends and had made such good friends that they could keep in contact.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: How did Pops feel about Bill being a conscientious objector?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: I don't know. I never discussed it with him.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: I need to ask him that.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: I just __________+ that Pops -- remembering and feeling more about the war now than you think that most of the men just _____________+.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: I do. I think they felt they had to. They had to move on so fast with their own lives.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: There was no choice but that.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And now --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: There was no sympathy of -- I say sympathy, but you know what I'm trying to say is they didn't -- so it is over now, we've won the war, let's get on with it.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Thanks for your duty, move on?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: That's right. I knew that is -- I do think they do that.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: And now that things have settled down and people are retiring, they have time to sort of think over their life?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: And relive their life. And there are so many -- in the last few years, they have noticed World War II more. And there are books out that they are buying, our age is buying.

You're trying to tell your children what -- what each one of you felt and went through during the time that it happened. I think each generation has something that they have to deal with. And I guess terrorists is a bad, bad thing because you never know where -- where that is or who that is where we had an enemy to fight and a place to fight. It has brought it home to us now.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: One thing I forgot to ask was -- I always thought that the women were given a job -- they were required to have a job to help service the --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: There was organizations that did make things for them that the women did. But at our age, it was mostly the older women. It was not the young ones. We were busy with our own -- going with the -- keeping the vow of family and working to support ourselves and then with children, when they did come back. But there were lots of efforts, yes. There were lots of efforts, but not from the immediate young ones.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did all of your girlfriends have babies as soon -- did you-all got pregnant at the same time?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Most of them did practically. That's the truth.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: I can imagine myself being selfish because I'd want to be -- everybody be excited for me being pregnant. And yet when everybody is having a baby --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Well, you know, misery loves company. You've always heard that expression. There was a lot of days that you didn't feel like eating and you had to eat. That was a real experience. Because I got pregnant with mine, and we were -- at that time, he was going to the university. So we ended up staying with the in-laws.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: And we had to -- she had a cook, and there was breakfast every morning. The cook came and cooked breakfast, and that was rough. I had to get up. I thought I should get up. ____________+. So up I got, and I went and ate and then I went to the bathroom.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: To throw up?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It was -- misery loves company. It was fun.
We -- the girls shared their --

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Get together and complain?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Yeah, complained about it. Oh, lord. But the shoes were the worst part of the rationing.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: You couldn't get all dressed up?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: You couldn't -- you had -- you had only so many coupons that you could use. So that was it. But you felt obligated before it expired to use it, whether you had found a pair of shoes. So you went and bought a pair regardless, because you knew you had to have some kind of shoe. But we ran into some great people, we really did.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: What money did you live off of when you got back?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: When he was gone?

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Well, when he got back. Did he work? Or were you --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: He couldn't really work.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: You were paid for his --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Yeah, his -- uh-huh. He had -- what do they call it?

Mustering out pay. And it -- then he went to school on the early part, on the -- the government paid for that. He did not get -- oh, I can't -- I haven't thought of the term. His injury was not compensated for.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Did he have to pay back -- was it loans that he was --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. It was not loans they -- I'm sure it was not loans. They just -- he was just paid. Of course families helped. My family always clothed the kids, you know. That was a big help, that kind of thing. Because we didn't require as much. We -- he was in school. And the facilities that we lived in, they had -- you could see the ground through the holes in the floor. But, you know, that was all right. It was a university thing, and we were lucky. We had two babies.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Just glad to have him back, too.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: And glad to have a place to sleep. Oh, yeah. That was funny. When we tried to furnish the first place, we didn't have any money that we could do these things, you know.
So we had to makeshift. At that time, they made paper draperies. They were heavy.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Like butcher paper?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: It was not butcher paper. It was printed. It was more of a paisley-type wallpaper, but it was a flimsy wallpaper that would ripple, you know. And that's what we went -- we had paper draperies in the windows, and we were lucky to have them. They had some pretty colors. We bought -- went to the Salvation Army, and we bought a cot and then we threw a blanket over it. It really was a bedspread.
And that was the cover. And then we add some cushions and tied some bows up with some fabric.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: That's where you slept?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: No. That was where -- that was our living room sofa.

We had a living room sofa. And then we selpt on the mattress that -- he had made a bed. And -- so that was fine. And we bought a mattress from this cheapy, cheapy place, which it was a real fatal mistake because that mattress was pretty raunchy.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Killed your back?

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Yeah. It didn't do much of anything. But gradually -- and then thanks to ____ and ______, they were generous and always bought us a chair or something for birthdays or Christmas. So it worked out fine. But we appreciated what we had because we didn't have anything.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: But we had each other, and that was par for the course. That was great.

sp.speaker: Wellon Lee
sp.p: It is probably frustrating for -- when your kids grew up not being so thrifty and --

sp.speaker: Emily Hays
sp.p: Well, no. The trouble is -- well, I think it just snowballs. When you don't -- you grow up not having everything -- I mean, a lot at your disposal, then you want to give more to your children. And each generation snowballs and snowballs. Because you love them so much, you want to do something for them. You want them to have everything they want, and it just snowballs. When you are just by yourself, you can makeshift. And I think you end up being a better person having to makeshift because then you appreciate everything because ______+.
